record.paper_title: Some open problems in mathematical relativity
record.original_question: What is the weakest regularity under which a vacuum metric can satisfy the Einstein vacuum equations, and how should one determine the optimal coordinates or best differentiable structure for such a low-regularity metric?

evidence.quote: Find the weakest possible regularity for a vacuum metric [CC;HKM;KT]. As observed by G. Huisken, the Ricci tensor is defined distributionally when the metric satisfies merely g,g-le L00 , Clge L2, so a metric satisfying only these regularity conditions could conceivably satisfy the (distributional) vacuum Einstein equations.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $(M, g)$ be a 4-dimensional Lorentzian manifold satisfying the vacuum Einstein equations $\mathrm{Ric}(g) = 0$. Classically one assumes $g \in C^2$ so that the Ricci tensor is defined pointwise. However, the Ricci tensor can be defined as a distribution under much weaker hypotheses: for instance, when in some coordinate chart $g, g^{-1} \in L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and the Christoffel symbols $\Gamma \in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$, the expression for $\mathrm{Ric}(g)$ makes sense in $\mathcal{D}'$.

Determine the weakest possible regularity (measured in suitable function spaces such as Sobolev, Hölder, or $L^p$-based scales for the metric, its inverse, the Christoffel symbols, and/or the curvature) on a Lorentzian metric $g$ under which:
(a) the vacuum Einstein equations $\mathrm{Ric}(g) = 0$ can be given a well-defined (distributional or otherwise) meaning, and
(b) a local existence/uniqueness theory for the Cauchy problem of the vacuum Einstein equations holds.

In addition, given such a low-regularity vacuum metric, describe how to choose an optimal system of local coordinates (or, more generally, a best differentiable structure on $M$) that maximizes the regularity of the metric components and is compatible with the distributional formulation of the equations.
artifact.status_search_result: Major progress has been achieved through the Bounded L^2 Curvature Conjecture, resolved by Klainerman, Rodnianski, and Szeftel (Invent. Math. 2015), which establishes that the time of existence of a classical solution to the vacuum Einstein equations depends only on an L^2 bound of the curvature and a lower bound on the volume radius of the initial data. This is critical (though not scale-optimal) regularity, since L^2 curvature bounds are the minimum required for control of the causal geometry. The fully optimal/scale-critical regularity threshold for vacuum metrics, and the determination of an optimal differentiable structure for such low-regularity metrics, remain open.

status_evidence.title: The bounded L^2 curvature conjecture
status_evidence.snippet: The time of existence of a classical solution to the Einstein-vacuum equations depends only on the L2-norm of the curvature and a lower bound on the volume radius of the corresponding initial data set.
status_evidence.claim: The L^2 curvature conjecture, a major step toward optimal vacuum regularity, was resolved.

status_evidence.title: The resolution of the bounded L2 curvature conjecture in general relativity
status_evidence.snippet: L2 bounds on the curvature is the minimum requirement necessary to obtain lower bounds on the radius of injectivity of causal boundaries.
status_evidence.claim: L^2 curvature is the minimum compatible with causal-geometric control, but full scale-critical regularity remains open.
